entities.summary:
Seulf, Archbishop of Reims from approximately 922 until his death in 925 CE, presided over one of the most prestigious and politically influential sees in West Francia during a period of profound Carolingian decline and aristocratic ascendancy. His brief but impactful tenure unfolded amidst the chaotic power struggles between the last effective Carolingian king, Charles the Simple, and a rising generation of powerful regional magnates, particularly Robert I and Herbert II of Vermandois. Seulf's position placed him at a critical nexus of spiritual authority and temporal politics, making his decisions and allegiances deeply significant for the stability of the realm and the autonomy of the Church.

During his archiepiscopate, Seulf was deeply embroiled in the ongoing conflicts that characterized early 10th-century West Francia. He was notably involved in the deposition of Charles the Simple in 922, a pivotal moment that saw the West Frankish nobility, led by Robert I, elevate one of their own to the throne. This act fundamentally challenged the hereditary principle of Carolingian rule. Seulf's participation, whether by direct action or implicit consent, underscored the Church's role as a kingmaker and legitimizer, capable of both upholding and undermining royal authority depending on its perceived interests or pressures from powerful lords. His predecessor, Hervé, had also navigated these treacherous waters, establishing a precedent for archiepiscopal engagement in royal succession.
